books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

stimulus.text:
This daguerreotype portrait of Frederick Douglass, made by Samuel J. Miller in 1847–1852, shows Douglass from the chest up, dressed as a respectable gentleman in a dark coat, white shirt, and bow tie, staring straight at the viewer with a stern expression.

"You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man." — Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845, on his fight with the overseer Edward Covey in August 1833.
stimulus.source_note: Portrait viewed before writing: Samuel J. Miller, daguerreotype of Frederick Douglass, 1847-1852, Art Institute of Chicago. Quotation verbatim from Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Miller daguerreotype of Douglass, 1847-1852, public domain
stem: The portrait shows Douglass dressed as a respectable gentleman and staring straight at the viewer. What does that presentation most directly do?

options.text: It proves Douglass had never been enslaved
options.misconception: Douglass escaped slavery in 1838; the portrait came later.

options.text: It answers racist caricatures with a dignified, commanding Black man
It shows Douglass was a wealthy plantation owner in Maryland
options.misconception: Douglass was born enslaved and became an abolitionist, not a planter.

options.text: It hides Douglass’s work as an abolitionist speaker
options.misconception: The stern, direct portrait advertises the speaker; it does not hide him.

rationales.A: The portrait cannot prove that. Douglass was born enslaved in Maryland and escaped in 1838.
rationales.B: Racist pictures showed Black people as servile or comic. Douglass answers with a dignified portrait, staring straight out.
rationales.C: Douglass owned no plantation. He was born enslaved and became a speaker and writer against slavery.
rationales.D: Nothing is hidden. A stern man in formal dress, staring at the viewer, is a speaker presenting himself to the public.
rationales.general:
1. Read the image. Dark coat, white shirt, bow tie, eyes straight at the viewer.
2. Ask what it argues against. Racist pictures showed Black people as servile or comic.
3. Name the move. Douglass used his own portrait to claim dignity in public.
Background: Douglass sat for over 160 portraits, more than Abraham Lincoln, and he managed his image with care.
Remember: a portrait is an argument; ask what it argues against.
